Mr. Chairman, mindful of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has said I will try to be as brief as possible. However I do wish to offer some remarks on the situation of the textile industry in this country, more particularly in my constituency, which includes the town of Drummond-ville where about 80 per cent of the people depend upon that particular industry for their living.
The government is well aware of the importance of this industry in the nation's economy. According to a report of the Primary Textile Institute 80,000 people are employed in this industry which ranks ahead of the iron and steel industry which employs
29.000	people and the pulp and paper industry which employs 62,000.
Besides the fact that its capital is 84 per cent Canadian, the textile industry also pays the highest wages in this country, averaging $1.20 an hour whereas in 1954, in Great Britain, the average hourly wage was 44 cents, as against 15 cents in Japan and 12 cents in India. The industry is further handicapped by competition resulting from British preferential tariffs.
At the present time, the Canadian textile industry supplies approximately 46 percent of the needs of the domestic market whereas last year the corresponding figure was 56 per cent. This 10 per cent decrease represents work which could have been carried out by our Canadian workers and, consequently, explains the present unemployment.
Comparing the present figures to last year's we find that the textile industry now employs
3.000	fewer people than it did then, which means 3,000 more unemployed. If we look at the situation in the Dominion Textile plant in Drummondville, we find that on November 2, 1957 there were 210 employees less than on November 3, 1956, a figure which must be considered in the light of the fact that that industry employs 1,000 people. There is unemployment therefore in Drummondville, as in every other community with
Interim Supply
a textile industry. That is why I felt that I should call the government's attention, this afternoon, to what, in my estimation, is a rather serious situation.
Two suggestions have been made in this connection by the Canadian association of textile manufacturers. To begin with there should obviously be a change in the definition of the word "dumping" which favours export of American products to Canada below cost price.
The Templon Spinning Mills Company, of Drummondville, sent a letter recently to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). Here is one paragraph from that letter:
(Text):
We suggest that an investigation of the declared price of American yarns being imported into this country be started. Templon Spinning Mills (Canada) Limited are prepared to provide your department with American orlon prices now in force in the United States, and we are sure that the rest of the Canadian synthetic spinners will be glad to supply similar information from their sources.
(Translation):
This clearly shows that the government must take action to correct the situation. If I felt justified in taking part in the debate this afternoon it is because I feel the matter to be urgent. I would have liked to speak at greater length but I will close now by asking the government to act as soon as possible.
(Text):

Had it not been for the recent remarks of the Minister of Finance I might have been disposed to remain silent and not utter the thoughts that crossed my mind this morning when he was giving us this usual solemn assurance about reserving the right to the committee to full discussion of the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, on the estimates.

However, having listened to his recent remarks I must remind him that at least two of his colleagues, namely the Prime Minister and the house leader, have been making very strong suggestions to us that they expected us to have completely dealt with the estimates prior to the Christmas recess. They have also been taking some steps to foreshorten the normal opportunities in this house to discuss some of the problems of the Canadian people under motions for supply. I feel, therefore, that perhaps it is not inappropriate that we should seize this occasion to raise such matters as have been raised by hon. members like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. Having said that, I assure the Minister of Finance I am going to express what I have to say as briefly as possible.

Interim Supply
My colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, attempted to offer some constructive suggestion as to how the immediate unemployment situation that has developed in some areas of the country be handled. I have a matter which I might normally have raised as a matter of departmental policy on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries, but in view of the urgency of the unemployment situation as described by my colleague the member for Vancouver-Kings-way I feel it can very appropriately be related to the remarks that were made by him, by the hon. member for Kootenay West and others. On two recent occasions I have made some mention in the house of the fact that on Vancouver island and in other parts of British Columbia there are more than the usual number of unemployed loggers as well as a large number of qualified construction workers who are now without jobs and seeking work. For that reason I should like to mention this as part of the national development policy about which the party to which the Minister of Finance belongs have been having quite a bit to say.
The Minister of Finance may or may not know that along the coastal area of British Columbia we have several hundred streams which are used by our Pacific salmon for spawning purposes. Some of these streams are in the more rugged and undeveloped parts of the Pacific coast. One of the facts that has often been brought out in reports by the federal Department of Fisheries is that, as a result of these streams being in undeveloped areas, nature continues to take its course so far as the facilities of the salmon for spawning are concerned. 1 have discussed on former estimates of the Department of Fisheries the reports that have been made that flash floods cause a loss of a good deal of the potential future salmon runs. In view of the unemployment situation amongst loggers and construction workers, now would be a very good time to undertake on a much larger scale than has heretofore been undertaken the development and improvement of our salmon spawning streams along the Pacific coast. This is the type of work for which the unemployed loggers and unemployed construction workers would be particularly suited. Much of this work could be done at low levels where there would not be any great difficulty in carrying on work during the winter, even though it might not be the most pleasant time of the year to do it.
The whole question of carrying on a development program which would have the effect of decreasing the damage caused salmon streams as a result of logging activity

when it is going at full blast is something that could be considered in a program of this kind.
As I said to the minister, Mr. Chairman, I intend to be as brief as I can in stating this point. But I do feel, in view of the unemployment situation which has been brought to the attention of the government and which probably will be brought to their attention to an increasing extent as the days go by unless something is done, that this is a practical sort of suggestion which could very well be carried out at this time. It is not the sort of thing which, as the hon. member for Kootenay West said, need divide us on partisan political lines but something which, as far as I can see, is a genuine suggestion to meet the immediate situation and provide employment opportunities to some of the people of British Columbia who at the present time have not got those opportunities.

Mr. Chairman, I notified the Minister of Finance that I wanted to discuss the earlier vesting of pension rights. It would take me about ten minutes to do so but I am willing to co-operate with his request in order that the work of the house may progress. I think I can deal with the matter later under his estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I fully appreciate the attitude of the Minister of Finance. Being here under the conditions I am and having regard to the position I occupied previous to coming here I suppose I should be one of the last to break either the rules of the house or its precedents. I do not intend to do that. So far as interim supply is concerned, I am quite willing to let the minister go ahead. Let us get on with the job, but there is one thing I should like to point out to him. I must protest the action he takes when he brings an interim supply motion before the house and does not give all members a list of what he proposes to do. He may say, of course, that he has not had time to prepare a list but I noted that he provided one for the leaders of each group and I suppose for each member of the cabinet. If that is possible, I suggest to him it is equally possible to mimeograph it and let all members have it.
After all we are not mind readers and when it comes to relating one-twelfth of an item that is in the blue book, plus the supplementary estimates, I put it to him that it requires quite a feat of mental acrobatics in order to be able to relate the one to the other. When he gets down into cents and tells us that one amount is one-twelfth of another amount of money it would be helpful if we could compare the two and make sure he is correct because, after all, we are policemen

so far as the Minister of Finance is concerned and we want to carry out our duties. I suggest to him that when he brings interim supply before the house in the future, as he probably will do, that he take steps to have all members provided with a list of the things that he proposes to do so that we will at least know what we are talking about.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I should take this opportunity provided by the motion for interim supply, representing one-twelfth of the total estimates of those departments which have not as yet been adopted, to bring to the attention of the house the acute unemployment situation in the city of Quebec and, more particularly, in the constituency of Quebec West.
If unemployment is now on the increase, it is due primarily to the Canadian people's lack of confidence in the present government. Another cause is the fact that the government has no definite policy but prefers to drift along and to attempt to take advantage of opportunities most likely to strike the voters' fancy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, again I must rise and appeal to my hon. friend and to the house. My hon. friend has indicated he is going to make a speech relating to a matter that can properly be raised on the estimates. Again I respectfully remind him that I have given to the house the assurance that these estimates will be open for discussion. The ministers of the various departments will be before the committee of supply with their estimates throughout the session and any speech that is relevant to any item of the estimates can be made. But, Mr. Speaker, we are just going to have duplication of debate if we are going to go on as we are today-just duplication.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have listened fairly regularly to the speeches which have been made since the beginning of this debate on interim supply. As members have spoken on just about everything, I do not see why I would be discriminated against and prevented from making a few remarks on the subject of unemployment.
At one time the western farmers could not sell their wheat so the house voted an amount of $150 million for cash advances. But what does the government propose to do about our unemployed? Is it planning to set up 20 cents a day camps again, as under the Bennett administration? What amount is the government planning to spend during the next four or five months? The government should not
Interim Supply
concentrate all its attention on the next election, but should be providing for women and children who will suffer from cold and hunger this winter.
The people in my constituency have done their share; when our country was threatened, they agreed to all the sacrifices called for by the authorities. Today the workers' families are facing the threat of unemployment, and it is our duty to help them in their hour of need. When our country was threatened, all our resources and all our wealth were drawn upon. Well, for goodness sake, let us do something for the worker's family!
In Quebec city, there are considerable and urgent works to be done, but unfortunately, the municipality cannot afford to undertake them. However, since there is very serious unemployment there, the federal government not only can but must carry them out as soon as possible.
There is first the cleaning up of the Lairet river and the dredging of the St. Charles river, two projects which were mentioned more than once in this house. The shores of the St. Charles river could be finished with ornamental stone in some attractive way, as was done in many other cities. This river runs through Quebec city and such works would greatly help beautify the city and would also help solve the unemployment problem.
May I also point out that the building of a post office would provide jobs for large numbers of workers. The government should urge the Canadian National authorities to settle this problem once and for all and then call for tenders at once.
It might be advisable to take again under consideration the proposal that old age pensions be payable at age 65 instead of 70. Workers forced to retire at 65, as happens in most cases, would thus have some means of support even if they were unable to lay anything aside while they held jobs. We all know that at the present time it is just about impossible for this class of people to find jobs. The old age pension should therefore be made universally payable at 65.
Also located in my constituency is the Savory Park hospital, in the municipality of Quebec West. Well, that institution even lacks an auditorium where patients could be entertained. There again, the works could be carried out during the winter. Among the patients are Hungarians and Eskimos, and it seems to me that we should provide them with recreational facilities which could not fail to relieve some of the bitterness they certainly feel in their heart not only as patients but as expatriates. Moreover, the northeastern side of the hospital is only

a few feet away from houses which the department of national health and welfare should expropriate so as to give the patients something better to look at, namely the city of Quebec.

I only wish to take a few moments of the time of the house to discuss a matter of urgency in the particular area of Canada from which I come, namely the prairie provinces. This really is a matter of urgency. We have heard a considerable amount of reference this afternoon to the subject of unemployment from members from all parts of Canada. It is a good thing for Canada, I think, that we are hearing these stories. It seems that the procedure of parliament is a little better than it was a year ago when we did not hear so much about conditions in the maritimes, particularly on the coast.
Of course we have been hearing stories of the emergency situation in the prairie provinces for a good many years. I cannot say that people in the prairie region are unemployed; they are busy and they have been busy. They have produced some tremendous crops; the only trouble with us is that while the men have been working, they have received no pay. Perhaps one of the causes has been the heavy crops and that Canada is not delivering its grain and has not been able to sell sufficient of its farm produce. The government is not getting rid of the grain, and as a result there is a backlog in the storage of grain in Canada today which is the greatest in the history of this country. The records will show that there is overstorage in the elevators, at the terminals and in the interior of the country; in almost every place in the prairies we have storage elevators filled to capacity.
The farmer in the past few years has not been able to deliver sufficient grain to pay his operating expenses; I would say not even

60 per cent of his operating expenses. Over the past four years we have been urging the government to undertake a job of building storage facilities in Canada which will take care of the grain left on the farm, grain which under the present conditions is spoiling, but the government has not seen fit to undertake such a program.
I would suggest to the government this afternoon that they could well undertake such a program of grain storage which would benefit a large number of people. However, first of all it would benefit the farmers who are unable to deliver their grain. At the present time the farmer is forced to try and make storage available, but in many cases he is unable to afford to do so. As anyone who has travelled across the prairies during the fall in the past few years will have noticed, there are piles of grain stacked in millions of bushels because there is not sufficient storage space for it. Grain piled in the open on the prairies or put into open bins because the farmer is already loaded to capacity cannot be left in such a way without a certain percentage of spoilage. The farmers' own bins are inadequate and there is a lot of spoilage due to the moisture leaking in at the sides.
This is a criminal waste in the first place, especially in a world where there are two billion people going hungry and it is a waste which should not be allowed to occur. Under the present circumstances the farmer has to take the loss in the form of spoiled grain which he cannot use and which is probably thrown away. He may be able to use a certain portion of it for feed but I am sure I am safe in saying there are millions of bushels each year wasted on the western prairies because of the lack of storage.
The providing of these facilities would do a lot of good; it would provide work for the unemployed and it would provide a use for our lumber. It would be a good thing for Canada generally because the figures show that as a result of improved efficiency more and more grain could be produced. Our average production over the years is increasing but there is a decline in the quantity which the country is able to sell.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce in reply to questions this afternoon indicated that the government has no program for disposal of surplus agricultural products to undeveloped countries where the people need it most. This is because these countries have no dollars with which to buy this food. Well I suggest to this government that the country should have a surplus agricultural disposal

policy which makes it possible to get rid of our surplus agricultural products.
If we in the democracies wish to show that we have something better than guns to offer to the world it would be a good thing for this country to formulate such a policy and undertake a program of such disposal to these countries. Give it to them. Today the farmer is losing it anyway; a lot of it is just wasted. It would be much better to give it away than to leave it where it is.
The government could undertake a program of giving to these countries which have no Canadian dollars the food they need to prevent them from suffering the starvation which faces them every day. We would, after all, be giving to those who need it a commodity of which Canada has so much. Aside from the humanitarian aspects of the situation, at least it would be better than letting it spoil.
On the other hand, if we had at least another 200 billion bushels' storage space in this country it could be used to capacity, and this would certainly relieve the situation as far as the farmer is concerned. The farmer is now forced to bear the brunt. As I say, he is employed all right but he gets no pay for his trouble. If he can sell another 300 million bushels this fall that would also relieve the situation considerably.
These farmers are in desperate straits with about 80 per cent of them hanging on the ropes and about 10 per cent having given up and left the farm. I urge this government to look deeply into this matter and they may find they can solve a number of problems. First of all they could provide some employment; secondly they could ease an industry which today is in desperate circumstances. I could tell stories of farmers who are trying to operate their farms, but because they have not been allowed to deliver their grain they have no money with which to pay their taxes. This has meant that the farmer has left the farm in the winter, leaving his wife and probably a couple of little children and the wife has had to feed the cattle and take care of the home while he goes to the bush or out to Kitimat to try to earn some money to keep the family going. He comes back in the spring and again puts in his crop in the hope that he will be able to hang on and deliver his grain and make a living out of the agricultural industry.
Surely it is not wrong that a farmer should be growing grain when the world is hungry. Surely Canada can play its part in seeing that these grain crops go to the hungry people of the world. The government knows that the present program of the Colombo plan is not enough. Other countries can
Interim Supply
get their surplus agricultural products out to the world; Canada should adopt a policy whereby she could take at least a portion of these surpluses and feed these people. Surely the government should be willing to undertake part of such an expenditure. I maintain it would be good defence for Canada to earn friends among the underprivileged nations of the world. We can waste billions of dollars on defence, upon armaments which are obsolete when delivered. Surely a portion of that money could be directed into the agricultural field to introduce a disposal program of our agricultural surplus products, and help to do away with the injustice which exists today in agricultural policies, and provide Canada with a food bank which may be useful in the years to come.
The former government made the mistake of constantly telling the house that everything was all right, that this was merely a temporary condition. I pointed out to the then minister of trade and commerce on more than one occasion that because of the conditions existing in the world today and because of the difficulties of our foreign markets the farmer was in a position where he was less and less able to deliver the grain he grows; and today grain deliveries are gradually resolving themselves into a mere trickle. I can show the committee farmers in the west who have to store grain grown three years ago. Today the grade is down because of the long period of storage. Who is taking that loss? Feed companies go around and offer farmers 60 cents a bushel for No. 3 wheat so they can make feed out of it within the province where the transaction does not come under the wheat board act. Again, the farmer is taking the loss. I do not know any other industry in which the cost-price squeeze has closed out the little fellow to the extent it has done in agriculture. What I have been suggesting is one way of making it possible for these people to carry on in the great work we are doing, the constructive and necessary work of growing food for a hungry world.

I think the attitude of the government is confirming, as the days go on, some of the things one hears around this building from members of the press and hon. members in all parties, namely that the government does not intend to bring in a budget before the next election, and that it is following a very deliberate policy of making certain that it shall not present a balance sheet to the people of this country. additional expenditure. We hear it suggested that there may be certain reductions in taxation, and the government has, in fact, promised that these reductions will be made. But I can tell him that the annual wheat pool convention to which he spoke was anything but satisfied with the presentation given to them by the minister, and they are anything but satisfied with the record of his own department and the record of the government in this field. I say that because I am informed, and I believe reliably informed, that not too long after the minister had made his speech and had left the annual meeting a very important resolution was passed. The resolution said that the Saskatchewan wheat pool organization should organize, unless there is an immediate change in government policy a mass delegation of people from Saskatchewan to Ottawa to interview the government and try to get it to change the disastrous course it is now following. The minister can rise in his place and he can contradict this statement and he can defend his position, if he can, but the fact is that in the present crop year as compared with the period in the crop year one year ago, about which his party complained so much, combined exports of all grains are down; prices are softening and the farmer's cost of production is going up.
The point is that the Saskatchewan wheat pool, a responsible organization, and one of the most important farm organizations in Canada and a very important part of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, was so displeased with the government's record in this field that they are considering the organization of a mass delegation to come to Ottawa. I believe the last time the Saskatchewan wheat pool organized a mass delegation was in 1942, when a delegation of some 400 farmers and businessmen came from the prairies to interview the government of the day to protest conditions at that time. The cycle is now apparently about complete. Unless this government changes its policy which today threatens the very existence of the agricultural industry in all parts of Canada, unless it does something to stabilize prices, as far

The exports of all of these grains for the same period this year have fallen to 90i

million bushels, or a drop of almost 22 million bushels in that period. Thus the government's export record is a dismal failure. Agricultural producers are finding that their income is falling.

We have witnessed today, I think, an extraordinary exhibition. A motion for interim supply, as hon. members who have sat in previous parliaments well know, has almost invariably been dispatched in a matter of about 15 minutes. In the 12J years I have been in this house I recall only one occasion where any discussion arose on a motion for interim supply, that is until this new parliament was elected and met in October. The position taken by my predecessors, three of them, who sat here in that time, has always been that the purpose of a motion for interim supply was simply to give the government the means necessary for carrying on for a limited period, usually one month. So far as discussion is concerned, the rights of all hon. members to say whatever may be pertinent or relevant under the rules of the house about any item are carefully preserved in the undertaking that the Minister of Finance always gives to the house. This is the assurance the house has that there will be no trespassing upon or diminution of the rights of the house to discussion.
It is for this reason also, Mr. Chairman, that ministers of finance have said that matters such as would be in order on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply or would be in order in the consideration of the items of the estimates in committee of supply ought not to be discussed on a motion for interim supply. What did we witness today? The hon. member for Coast-Capilano, the financial critic of the official opposition, spoke and indicated that the official opposition would support the motion and would not extend the discussion. Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, speaking as it appeared for the C.C.F.

group in the house, said that his group was supporting the motion because they realized the government must have something with which to meet expenses. He was extraordinarily brief and said, as he sat down, that there were three members of his group who would speak very briefly on individual matters.

urgent business on the order paper as the government is asking the house to do.

Members are being given more information this session in this respect than they have ever been given before. In the time-honoured practice of the house on matters of interim supply, as long as the leaders of the parties are satisfied the vote has gone through without interminable discussion.
I was asked today about the intentions of the government with respect to the items that are to appear before the house in committee of supply in due course. Reference was made to what has happened already on the estimates of the two departments that have been before the house in committee of supply. Here let me very briefly draw attention to precisely what happened. On November 20, when the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State were before the house the Secretary of State, when asked whether the house was to be asked to vote in full the amounts of the estimates of her department, said, as found at page 1340 of Hansard:
-having regard to the commitments which have already been undertaken by the department, I think that in so far as my own department is concerned it would be advisable to ask for the votes as they stand and then effect what economies we can rather than try to cut regardless of the requirements of the department and then be forced to ask for some of that cut-back in supplementary estimates at a later date.
Let it be remembered that all the items involving salaries in that department have been increased by reason of the general increase in salaries in the civil service and even with that the Secretary of State is pointing out that she is managing to finance on the estimates without making special provision for additional supplementaries.
When my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, brought his estimates before the house on November 21 he prefaced his statement on that occasion by referring directly to the matter of reductions in

the items in his department, and he said, as recorded at page 1380 of Hansard:
Since the date of my appointment as minister of this department I have carefully examined these estimates, together with my officers, and as a result it has been found possible to divert approximately $500,000 to other requirements which were not foreseen at the time these estimates were prepared. Specifically, about $250,000 was used to help defray the cost of the general salaries revision of May 1, 1957, and a smaller amount was used to assist in settling accounts resulting from the grounding of the C.G.S. Baffin in July, 1957. Hon. members will appreciate that had this action not been taken it would have been necessary to request additional funds by way of supplementary estimates in order to cover these items.
It will be seen, Mr. Chairman, that the ministers have been dealing with this matter of effecting reductions in the estimates of their departments where that can be done without sacrificing any essential service and the house has been acquainted with the results. That practice will be followed as the estimates of succeeding departments are considered by the house in committee of supply.
There is one matter that was raised by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet today and was also touched on by two other members. It was the position of the textile industry. I am not going to say anything more than is strictly required in reply to what was said by these hon. members. The textile industry has been faced with difficult conditions in recent years. This matter is raised by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet today as though he had made a new discovery.
It is the first time that the mill at Montmagny has closed down for lack of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend-
Under a Tory regime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-that the matter has been a subject of very keen concern to those of us who are now sitting on this side of the house for a long time, and while one will have the greatest concern about the closing of any mill I am glad to see that some hon. members opposite have now discovered for the first time that there is this problem in the textile industry. I can well remember when I was on the other side of the house raising this question time after time after time and pointing to the difficulties of the textile industry. Did we receive any support from the hon. members who now form the official opposition and who spoke today? Never a word, Mr. Chairman; never a word did we hear from them, never an indication of concern.
But now they are beginning to discover the problem. This is a problem that is giving the government concern as it gave members now

sitting on this side of the house great concern when they sat in the opposition and when it gave the former government no evident concern.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It did very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The government of that day made a reference to the tariff board of the woollen items in the tariff. That was done three years ago, and what did they do? It was a truncated inquiry that they directed the tariff board to make. They told the tariff board not to make any recommendations. So the tariff board simply made a review of conditions in the industry so far as woollen textiles were concerned and made no recommendations, and to this day we have had no recommendations.
What the new government did in the face of the problem was to direct the tariff board to proceed with an inquiry into the whole textile industry embracing all the textile items in the tariff. The tariff board has proceeded with the inquiry with respect to the woollen items. They have completed their hearings and they are working on their report now. I shall be very interested indeed to see what kind of reception the recommendations of the tariff board in this respect, whatever they may be, receive from hon. members opposite when they come.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, there is one thing that must be mentioned here in the light of statements that have been made today, principally by the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet and the hon. member for Essex West. Apparently they are seeking to create the impression that the government trade mission now in the United Kingdom is seeking to make purchases which are going to have the effect of depriving Canadian workmen of jobs. Let us scotch that ugly apparition right now. It has been made clear by the government from the outset that the policy of seeking to divert purchases to Britain applies purely and exclusively to purchases of goods now made elsewhere outside Canada.
Let it not be pretended by hon. members opposite that in this trade mission or in its purpose there is any threat to the jobs of Canadians. That fact appears to have been realized by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition when, on the eve of departure of the trade mission for the United Kingdom three weeks ago, that hon. gentleman wished them well and spoke-as we thought-for all members of the official opposition in applauding their efforts and wishing them success.
Nobody thought they would buy textiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There were also some statements from the two other groups in the house
Interim Supply
wishing the mission well, applauding their efforts and wishing them success. What has happened now? The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet says that the presence of several Canadian textile manufacturers in the trade mission-
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -seems to give rise to the suspicion that the mission is going to be engaged in the purchase of textiles over there which could be purchased in Canada. Mr. Chairman, did you ever hear anything quite so far-fetched? I would have thought that the best guarantee that there is going to be no injury done to the jobs of any Canadian textile worker or to the interests of any Canadian textile mill lies in the fact that there are Canadian textile manufacturers in the trade mission.
No there are not. They are importers not manufacturers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We were told-
Look at the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We were told this morning that there were representatives of the textile industry in the group.
Garments manufacturers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think that by looking at the composition of the trade mission and if the hon. members will only hearken back to what their own leader has said, they will have ample assurance that there is nothing in the activities of this trade mission which need give concern to Canadian industry or Canadian workmen. It has been made clear by the government from the very outset -and the facts should not be misrepresented now

that the policy of diversion applies purely and simply to goods now being purchased in other markets abroad.
Would the hon. minister permit a question? In view of what he has said, what about the purchase of generators and other electrical apparatus announced by Mr. Duncan, the leader of the mission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry I did not hear all of my hon. friend's question.
How about the announcement of the purchase of electrical apparatus made by Mr. Duncan, the leader of the mission? There was to be $10 million worth bought in Britain.

$10 million worth of generators purchased in Britain by the Ontario hydro.

Interim Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know the details of the particular purchase referred to, but I do know that the Ontario hydro electric power commission has previously made purchases in the United Kingdom of heavy electrical equipment not manufactured in this country, and I expect that Mr. Duncan has proceeded on that basis. I put it to the hon. members opposite that if the words of their leader uttered in this house on the occasion of the departure of this mission represent the feeling of the hon. members opposite, then these statements which have been made today obviously are hollow and have no place in the language of the official opposition. On the other hand, if the right hon. Leader of the Opposition was not speaking for them when he wished the mission well three weeks ago then, in fairness to him and in frankness to the house I urge them now to declare it.
I did not intend to review these matters; I have spoken as I have simply to put the facts straight in the light of a number of statements made here today. I deplore the fact that these matters have been raised at all on a motion for interim supply and I appeal to the house-
Appeal!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -to address our efforts to the purpose of the matter in hand. There will be plenty of opportunity to discuss these matters when other business is before the house. The undertaking has been given that the rights of hon. members to discuss these matters and any others relative to any items in the estimates will be preserved and surely the matter can rest there.

I would like to address a question to the minister as to whether he is stating government policy or whether that policy was stated this morning by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I ask this because the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated repeatedly this morning that there were no restrictions whatsoever upon this particular mission as to what they should purchase so far as the government was concerned. The Minister of Finance is saying the very opposite at this time. Who is speaking for the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance is not saying the opposite to what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce but is saying something which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said before and which is government policy shared by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself, as it is by all other members of the government. I think my hon. friend knows that.

I would like to ask further to the question raised by the hon. member for Dauphin, are the members of this mission honour bound to discuss while they are overseas on a trip at the expense of Canada only the purchase over there of commodities that would be in the diversion field rather than those which are of domestic availability.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, surely there will be a proper opportunity to go into this whole question-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You invited this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -will probably be before the house at the end of this week because the Minister of Trade and Commerce will be returning, as he indicated in his statement on Tuesday, to the United Kingdom to complete the work of the trade mission. His estimates will be before the house and surely that is the proper place to raise these questions and go into them as fully as any hon. member may wish.
You raised it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not raise it. 1 was setting the facts right as I made clear to the hon. members in view of the statements which have been made here and which were at variance with the facts. Conclusions have been reached and inferences drawn which the facts do not warrant. These were all contrary to the position taken by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and I was speaking in an effort simply to put the record straight. As I have said, I deplore the fact that a discussion of this kind had been obtruded into a debate on interim supply.
You are delaying interim supply.

I was sure the hon. minister had suggested that the occupation of the delegation was simply that of trade which had the purpose of diversion from the United States. Discrimination against the United States.

I would like to put the record straight too, Mr. Chairman, in one particular. No minister of the crown can sit over there and threaten us in any way whatsoever but if there are to be threats we can threaten just as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no question of any threats.

If so, he is
guilty of acting with calculated insolence. If he is querying our rights to speak here whenever we want to do so, he had better have a change of mind because I recall when the hon. member sat on this side of the house he spoke talkatively, loquaciously, verbosely, wordily and with much repetition, boring us all to death with his long speeches. Now he has the impertinence to ask us to simmer down, to calm down. He wants us to exercise forbearance with respect to his party's policy. Not likely. We are not prepared to exercise forbearance with growing unemployment as it exists in this country and with the situation as it now exists, where thousands of farmers are being dispossessed of their farms and their homes because of a lack of policy on the part of this government. Furthermore, I did not like this other threat that if we did not cooperate-
Might I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly, ask any questions you like.

How are you
assisting the passing of the legislation to help farmers or to help unemployment problems to be solved by continuing this unnecessary discussion?

We assisted in passing unemployment legislation by putting it through in less than one day. When we talk about assisting in legislation, if this farm legislation is as important as the government thinks it is, why, then, did the order of business include the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act? Why the Export Credits Insurance Act, if the farm legislation is so urgent? Why the Hamilton harbour commission measure if the farm legislation is so important? Why the Canadian Vessel Construction Assistance Act if the farm legislation is so important?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is employment involved in very one of these measures.

Why has the
government been stalling for over a month on this matter, and why does the Minister of Finance then tell us that if we do not cooperate the leader of the house will be guided accordingly? I do not like these threats, nor do my colleagues and we are not prepared to take them from anyone. We are here today to do a job as we see it, though perhaps we do not see eye to eye with the government, and when any of my colleagues want to speak in this house they will do so.
96698-118i
Interim Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then let us have no talk about delaying matters.

When the Prime Minister was on this side of the house we used to hear how interested he was in freedom of speech, but now he is Prime Minister he wants to act the part of R. B. Bennett and clamp down upon discussion, and we are not prepared to take it. The Minister of Finance said that the house was going to be in session for a long time. Well, we are paid to be here, and the hon. minister is paid to be here; we are going to be here as long as he will be, and in all probability longer. May I give this advice to the hon. gentleman: if he wishes to facilitate the business of this house, let him stop making these threats and speak more courteously and with greater regard for the rights of hon. members of parliament.

Mr. Chairman, the minister spoke for some considerable time, and the last part of his speech, in which he was answering questions, was, I think, quite acceptable, though he did enter into debate on those things which he claimed were taking a lot of the time of the committee.
But in answering these questions he did not answer the question I asked him and which, I thought, dealt with an important matter. I asked him what estimates he thought might be withdrawn, because that is pertinent to debate. One reason I spoke on the coal mining industry during this debate was because I anticipated that the estimates in respect of the dominion coal board would not come before this parliament, and I had to take the opportunity to speak on that subject when it was presented to me. I asked the Minister of Finance to tell us what estimates would be withdrawn or curtailed; and while he is on his feet, would he care to answer me with respect to my speech? He has referred at some length to speeches which were made in respect of the trade mission. But to me and to my people the coal mining industry is more important than that, and I should like the minister to tell me what the government proposes to do to assist the coal mining industry in its present difficulties. The other question I asked was whether the minister will tell us what estimates may be withdrawn or curtailed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I dealt with that subject in the course of my remarks and I referred to the practice which had been followed already by the two ministers whose estimates have been before the committee of supply and passed, and I said that this would be the practice followed by each minister as he places his estimates before the committee

Interim Supply
of supply, namely that he would indicate what particular revisions he thinks could be made in his estimates. I can assure the hon. member that he will have ample opportunity to discuss the important subject he has raised on the estimates which are still to come before the house.

I have just one word to say. A few moments ago the Minister of Finance, when he began replying to the various speeches which had been made, introduced his remarks by saying that a discussion of more than 15 minutes on interim supply was something quite out of the ordinary; that in the 12 years he had been in the house, only once according to his memory had a debate gone longer than about 15 minutes.
I can assure him that the debates on interim supply have been longer than his memory. His memory is very bad, and I am really concerned for the finances of the country if his recollection cannot do any better than that, because not later than last spring there were two instances when there were protracted debates on interim supply. On April 11, 1957, the then minister of finance moved interim supply. The present Prime Minister spoke at considerable length- as a matter of fact his speech covers a number of pages of Hansard-and it was only on the following day at six o'clock that the interim supply motion was adopted. In that same session, on March 29, 1957, interim supply was moved by the former minister of finance on a Friday morning at 11 o'clock and it was only around five o'clock that the motion was approved. On that occasion the present Minister of Finance in his capacity as the hon. member for Eglinton made a long speech, of the character which was described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, on the subject of the C.B.C. For 40 minutes the hon. member spoke on the C.B.C. and his speech covered seven pages of Hansard.
What page was that?
Page 2022 of Hansard for the first session of 1957.
Did it happen in any other year?
I did not have time to check, because it is only a few moments ago that the Minister of Finance said it had happened only once-
Once in 12 years.
He said it had never happened.
Once in 12 years.

I did not have to go any further back than the spring session to find

that the Minister of Finance had participated in a protracted debate on interim supply.
Once in 12 years.

Mr. Chairman, I want to assure the Minister of Finance that the lecture he delivered to the house a few moments ago has not intimidated me in the least with regard to saying the few words I have to say at this time.
I feel I am not abusing my rights and privileges if I speak at this time, and while I certainly appreciate the suggestion of the hon. minister that we will have an opportunity during the discussion of the estimates at a later date to bring up our several grievances which have been mentioned here this afternoon, the minister did not say when the estimates are going to be brought up and as I have something to say relevant to the problem of storage I feel I am perfectly within my rights at this time in airing that grievance. On the other hand, if the minister will assure me now that he will bring before this house the support price legislation tomorrow or the next day I will resume my place immediately and say nothing at this time.
Now who is threatening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is well aware of the order of business which was announced by the leader of the house last night, and he is well aware that this agricultural price guarantee legislation is among the items announced last night for today. It was our expectation on this side of the house that we should have been about that business by this time.

Now you
are reneging on the problem.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to belabour the point except to say that on a number of occasions hon. members in this corner of the house have pleaded with the government to dispense with relatively unimportant legislation in order to facilitate the bringing forward of important legislation including the price support legislation. Neither this morning nor this afternoon did the minister suggest that members of the government should not participate in the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only one member on the government side of the house spoke, only one.
You made a long speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When?
Now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I spoke only five minutes this morning.

I would like to say a few words concerning the serious problem that was raised by the hon. member for Yorkton. I am not going to abuse the privileges extended to me by quoting figures concerning storage because they are as well known to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to anyone else but I would like to deal with one aspect of the problem which heretofore has not been brought to the attention of the house. I am sure the minister is as anxious as anyone else to do everything possible for the agricultural industry of Canada.
Thank you very much.

The minister has made many statements to that effect although I must admit that we have not seen too much action to date. On one occasion I recall he said in effect he did not believe producers should be asked to carry the entire burden of the surplus grain problem and on another occasion in this house, as I recall it, he said in effect that the government was prepared to consider any reasonable plan that would help alleviate many of the present problems of the agricultural industry. And so, believing that, I would like to bring to his attention one such problem, namely storage, which could be assisted somewhat by using one piece of legislation that is presently in force in this country.
I would point out to the minister that there already exists a policy which if it were extended would go a long way in at least attempting to solve the grave problem of grain storage. I understand that there has been no off-site storage approved since approximately June 25 of this year but since that date on-site or on-track storage has been approved, which of course is something entirely different.
On November 18 I asked the minister a question to the effect that if a group of farmers or an individual farmer constructed approved on-site storage at an elevator point would he be eligible to have that storage approved in effect by the Canadian wheat board which operates under the jurisdiction of the federal government. The minister's answer to me as reported at page 1231 of Hansard of that date is as follows:
The board of grain commissioners will only accept applications for on-site storage from licencees of the board.
Interim Supply
Later he added:
In other words, such on-site storage is regarded as an annex to the elevator licensed to receive grain at that delivery point.
It is evident from those statements that the question I asked the minister on that occasion was answered in the affirmative. The only result of that policy that I can observe from having investigated the situation quite carefully is that in certain areas businessmen who are constructing approved or already have approved existing storage make a deal with an elevator company and in turn are paid storage charges on that grain. I am not at all critical of any businessman who provides storage for housing grain because I think it is most admirable, nor am I critical of the wheat board or this government for approving that type of storage but I do condemn the government for not publicizing as widely as possible the existence of this scheme and the fact that farmers can take advantage of the plan.
How does this plan work? I will give a concrete example concerning a situation that is well known to me. A businessman has storage capable of housing 100,000 bushels. He goes to an elevator company and makes a deal which is perfectly legitimate under which he will store grain on their behalf and in return he is paid something in the neighborhood of three-quarters of a cent per bushel. It is understandable of course that he could not qualify for the full cost of storage because the elevator company must deduct handling charges which amount to about one-quarter of a cent per bushel. That is all very well and it means that at this point farmers have an extra 100,000 bushels of storage capacity but it would be much better if the government would publicize this scheme in order that farmers could take advantage of this scheme.
I have it on the best authority that there are elevator companies who would be very happy to enter into such an arrangement. Farmers could undertake to arrange on-track storage and build their own storage to store their own grain as the quota became available. In this case they would be paid storage just as the businessman is paid storage today.
What would be accomplished by this? It would accomplish three things, all of them desirable. First of all, because there would be greater storage at that point, the quota could be raised which in turn would mean that the farmer would be able to market more grain at that point. He would be able to haul his grain and put it in his granary without fear of the elevator being plugged. You must remember that simply because a quota is opened at any point it does not mean that every farmer will have an opportunity

Interim Supply
of getting his grain into the elevator. In many cases there is difficulty because of weather conditions and so on and the elevator space is plugged before the farmer can make his delivery. This would eliminate the second problem.
The third thing it would accomplish would be to give the farmer an opportunity to deliver grain to the elevator of his choice. For example, if he hauls it to a pool elevator he eventually gets the benefit of the dividends that are invariably paid which would be of great assistance. I suggest it would be much better for ten farmers to have 1,000 bushels apiece in their own bins on-track than to give that amount of storage to one man thereby putting him in the position of being able to collect the storage on all the grain.
Possibly the government feels that if this policy were widespread and expanded it would not be able to carry all the charges that would have to be borne. Of course the government has agreed to pay all the storage charges on what it considers to be over a normal carryover, 178 million bushels, but it is understandable that if this policy I am outlining now became widespread that it could conceivably amount to a vast quantity of grain on which the government would have to pay storage. In spite of that I think the plan is valid because the farmer is already carrying storage on the grain that is stored on his own farm but he is never sure he is going to be able to deliver when the quota does open up. Therefore I feel this policy should be expanded and the plan made widely known through the grain growing portion of western Canada. I know the government is not going to build permanent storage, I would suggest that as an alternative, and in the meantime they should give very serious consideration to allowing farmers the opportunity to build on-site storage wherever it is possible to do so.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that hon. members are very anxious to get these interim estimates through.
We were, but not now.
Oh, oh!

I hear a lot of laughter from across the way, but I want to assure you, sir, that neither I nor my colleagues will be intimidated by any laughter. I listened to the prolonged and verbose circumlocution of the Minister of Finance. I have a problem to bring to the attention of the government and I intend to do so in the remaining few minutes. If I do not get too many interjections from hon. members opposite, I think I can do it.

This problem, Mr. Chairman, applies perhaps more particularly to my own constituency. It has to do with the administration of two acts, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I bring this to the attention of the government because I believe it involves interdepartmental arrangements for carrying out the regulations of the two acts.
As hon. members know, under the Unemployment Insurance Act, unless a person is an industrial worker and within the two years prior to application for unemployment insurance benefits has paid a total of 30 weeks into the insurance fund he is not eligible for benefits. I bring this to the attention of the government because in my constituency we have a large group of people who are engaged in the oil industry because that area of the province of Saskatchewan is perhaps the largest oil field in Canada at the present time. Whether or not this is due to the new policy and the failure to take proper steps to give assurance to the industry and the oil companies that the future holds something for them in the way of further investment I am not sure, but the committee will recall that I asked the Prime Minister to give information to the house on the outcome of the visit of Premier Manning to the Prime Minister in respect of the oil situation in Alberta.
In addition to this, sir, we have the cost-price squeeze facing our farmers. Owing to the cost-price squeeze, and the lower return to farmers, many of them have gone into the oil fields and some of them are also working in the coal mines. For the information of the committee I might say that approximately half the coal of Canada is produced in my constituency. The problem is this. People who are employed part-time in the coal mines and in the oil industry and who have not completed 30 weeks of employment in either of those industries in the last two years are not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. At the same time we have the anomaly of people who are part-time farmers and who pay into the Prairie Farm Assistance Act through deductions on the sale of their grain. Such people are not eligible under the regulations of these two acts for compensation under either one of the acts. I should like to bring this to the attention of the government. Owing to the peculiar circumstances these people are not eligible under the regulations of the two acts. I hope the minister will bring it to the attention of the proper authorities that we have people who are paying into both the unemployment insurance fund and the Prairie

Farm Assistance Act but, owing to the regulations, they cannot qualify as industrial workers and are not eligible for payments under the Unemployment Insurance Act. They do not receive any compensation and they cannot qualify under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act because they are not classified as bona fide farmers. They are not eligible for awards under this act.
I would suggest to the government that a great deal of leniency be shown in the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so that people who are trying to supplement their incomes and find it very difficult to carry on, but are doing what I think all of us want them to do, namely try to find work to provide for their families, shall be eligible for payments and awards made under one or the other of those acts.
I think it is a real problem. I appreciate that the administrators of the Unemployment Insurance Act are trying to do the best they can. I think those who are carrying out the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are very sympathetic, and I do hope that my plea this afternoon will be given serious consideration and that people in this category will receive the proper consideration because in most instances it is a real problem in my constituency.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR CONVERSION OF CAPITAL STOCK COMPANIES INTO MUTUAL COMPANIES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, December 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming for the second reading of Bill No. 169, to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act.
Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Kenora-Rainy
River): Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of yesterday's sittings the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had finished his explanation of the reasons for this bill. With the background for the bill as he outlined it I have little dispute. I think the minister himself would probably be quite willing to acknowledge that much of the investigation and preparation for the bill had been done and was ready for him when he assumed office because I know from my personal experience, having been parliamentary assistant to the former minister of finance, that this matter had been given study by the previous minister and a draft bill had even been prepared.
However, the last session, as we all know, was brought to a conclusion sooner than some other sessions by reason of dissolution. My remarks will be brief not only on that account but also because the minister has assured the house that the bill will be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce. I should like, however, to join with him in acknowledgment that the bill is of considerable importance.
The insurance industry is an important one and, as the minister himself stated, the welfare of a great number of Canadians in a very important way is dependent upon our insurance industry. My understanding is that there are some 28 insurance companies operating in Canada which have jurisdiction by reason of incorporation by parliament and those companies, for whom we are legislating in this bill, write some two-thirds of the insurance that is written in Canada for Canadians. That totals some $26 billion or $27 billion and that, of course, underlines and emphasizes the security element that was referred to by me and by the minister last night.
Of the 28 companies I believe that 22 are companies with capital stock and these are the companies to which the element of mutualization in this bill has particular reference. I also believe that these companies with capital stock underwrite about 85 per cent of the business in this country.

Insurance Companies Act
Another factor that I think will be kept very much in mind by members of the house is the fact that it is not easy today to enter afresh into the business of insurance. I think only one company has entered this field of business in the last 25 years. The minister also indicated very properly last night that the funds of shareholders are relatively small in relation to the funds that are available to these insurance companies from the premiums that are provided by policyholders. The last time I have a recollection of looking at these figures I believe that the assets available to these companies were in the neighbourhood of $6 billion and this in turn can be related to paid up capital stock approximating $14 million.
I think the chief item in the bill of particular interest is the opportunity to facilitate mutualization. In that respect the bill is not proposing something that is particularly unique because in the United States they have developed something along the lines proposed in the bill. The two largest United States companies in the insurance field, the Metropolitan Life and the Prudential Life, were originally stock companies but they too, as is provided in this bill, became mutual companies by reason of an opportunity provided to purchase the capital stock of their companies. In addition, other United States companies formerly stock companies have been mutualized, including the New York Life and the Equitable Life. A similar trend has also been noted in the United Kingdom.
I think the bill provides a share of supervision on behalf of the public by reason of the reference in the bill to the jurisdiction of the treasury board. I think this will commend itself to most members of the house. There is another important element in the bill, the direction that the majority of directors must be residents of Canada. Up to now the direction has simply been that the shareholders' representatives on the boards of directors where there is participation, shall be residents of Canada, but this will apply now to all classes of directors. This again is not unique in legislative action because it is similar to the direction that is made with respect to the directors of our Canadian banks.
The third item that I think is of interest is the provision affording the opportunity for the boards of directors of our insurance companies to refuse share transfers to nonCanadian residents under certain circumstances. This, I think, is a matter that has given considerable concern to a number of Canadians in the past. I know the superintendent of insurance has directed the
attention of the house to this problem. In his 1955 report he had this to say:
One may, perhaps, feel less concern in contemplating these two transactions-
He was referring to certain transactions respecting sales of shares in insurance stock companies to non-residents.
-than would be the case were there to be a transfer of ownership of one of the major Canadian companies.
The Minister of Finance referred to certain control that has already passed from this country.	The superintendent of insurance
went on to say:
The transactions serve to emphasize the continued interest of foreign investors in Canadian life insurance companies and the desirability of seeking some legislative procedure that will enable the ownership of Canadian life insurance companies to be retained in Canada.
This problem also received the attention of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, and in paragraph 20 of the preliminary report of the Gordon commission the following was stated:
Foreign ownership of the stocks of the Canadian chartered banks and of life insurance companies, which are incorporated under Canadian law, is not particularly large at the present time. It is desirable that Canadian control of these institutions be maintained. The commission suggests, therefore, that appropriate action be taken to prevent any substantial measure of control of the chartered banks and of the life insurance companies from coming into the possession of non-residents. One way in which this might be accomplished would be to provide by statute that any shares in such institutions which were acquired by non-residents of Canada in the future would be ineligible to vote.
That of course is not the actual procedure adopted by this bill. I think it is not generally understood, however, that the provisions of the bill simply provide discretionary power on the part of the board of directors of an insurance company to refuse the transfer of shares to a non-Canadian resident. In addition, it is probably not understood that the bill does not provide that shares, once in the hands of a non-resident, can be transferred to another non-resident; not only at the present time but that this will be also possible in the future.
The fourth element of the bill referred to last night by the minister relates to the fraternal societies which effect insurance and I think there will be no quarrel with respect to that because it is generally recognized today that the unusual mortality rates which applied years ago to juveniles are not now prevalent. I think this bill should commend itself generally to the members of this committee; it seems to have general acceptance, so far as I know, by the members of the official opposition. Certainly such small differences as do exist can be discussed and the bill
itself will be given very careful examination by the committee on banking and commerce.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE TOTAL OUTSTANDING LIABILITY
speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment, is to increase the effectiveness of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation by giving it the necessary authority to take on liabilities of an additional $100 million, under section 21 of the Export Credits Insurance Act. Contracts of insurance issued under section 21 of the act are those which are considered to be in the national interest but which, in the opinion of the board of directors of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, would impose upon the corporation a liability for a term or in an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one contract, exporter, commodity or country. All moneys required by the corporation to discharge its liabilities arising under any contract of insurance entered into under this section are to be paid to the corporation by the Minister of Finance out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund.
Section 21 of the act as it now stands limits the corporation's liability to $100 million. At the present time, liabilities under policies of insurance actually written plus commitments currently outstanding total $98 million in the aggregate. It is obvious that in order to have this section of the act continue its effectiveness, and to allow the corporation to insure additional business, it must be authorized to assume further liabilities, and I am therefore proposing that the amount of such liabilities be established at $200 million.
Through the operations of section 21 of the Export Credits Insurance Act an increasing amount of export trade has been insured and a considerable portion of it would not have materialized had it not been possible to have it insured. One hundred and six policies of insurance have been issued under this section covering exports amounting to $206 million. Insured export shipments which have been concluded and paid in full amount to $97 million. Insurance premiums paid on this business have totalled $1,659,191 of which $1,245,488 has been turned over to the

Export Credits Insurance Act receiver general and the balance of $413,703 retained by the corporation to meet its expenses and overhead arising out of the contracts of insurance issued under section 21 of the act. I am pleased to report that as yet there have been no losses.
Shipments insured under section 21 have consisted of electrical goods valued at $4J million; milk powder valued at $4 million; aircraft and parts, $80 million, and wheat, $118 million.
In connection with the insurance of aircraft and parts amounting to $80 million, the corporation has assumed a liability of only $22 million. This has been brought about through the very favourable payment terms established in the contract of sale whereby it has been calculated that the maximum possible loss could not exceed the $22 million established as the liability. With respect to payment terms for other commodities insured under section 21, it is usual procedure for the exporter to receive some cash with the order, or at the time of shipment, with the balance payable over some months or years after shipment. Terms of payment for wheat sales insured have called for a cash payment of from 10 per cent to 25 per cent at the time of shipment with the balance payable from one to three years after the date of shipment.
Ordinarily wheat is sold for cash in international trade and, as the house is well aware, the Canadian wheat board requires payment in cash so that it can distribute the proceeds of sale to producers. Until 1952-and this act has been in operation since 1944-there were no requests for credit terms on the sale of Canadian wheat. In that year, Yugoslavia faced a serious shortage of food and foreign exchange and applied to Canada for wheat on short term credit. The private exporters financed themselves at commercial rates of interest through the banking system, using the export credits insurance policy as security, in order to pay cash to the wheat board.
With changes from time to time in credit terms this pattern of export insurance, worked out for this first transaction with Yugoslavia, has been applied in subsequent years to several other countries-Brazil, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Israel and Poland. Policies have been issued covering the export of 1J million tons, or about 55 million bushels of wheat.
As a result of recent intensive efforts to enlarge wheat markets, a number of countries have expressed interest in buying Canadian wheat on credit. At this stage it would not, of course, be in the public interest to disclose the names of the countries but it is vitally important that authority should be available (Mr. Churchill.]

to insure such credit sales if and when formal requests are made. That is the principal reason for seeking this amendment.
The Export Credits Insurance Corporation provides a service that cannot be obtained from private insurance firms. Similar insurance protection is provided by government of the majority of exporting countries. Export credits insurance gives protection to Canadian exporters against those unexpected and unpreventable losses that occur in spite of every precaution of the policyholder. Some of the risks covered include insolvency of the foreign buyer, cancellation of an import licence in the country of destination, or the risk of adverse changes in foreign exchange regulations. While the corporation will insure against delays in collection that are not the fault of the exporter, it does not cover trade disputes as to quantity of goods.
The exporter is insured against blockage of funds in a foreign country or transfer difficulties which prevent him from receiving payment for his goods. Such calamities as war or revolution in the country of the buyer are also covered. This insurance protection in no way subsidizes the Canadian exporter, as the corporation operates on a self-supporting basis and charges an insurance premium that is assessed according to the risk assumed. The Canadian exporter still has to compete on the basis of quality, price, credit terms, and service rendered. However, the policy of insurance provides protection for his foreign accounts receivable and also provides him with the benefit of the advice and assistance of the corporation in recovering any losses which may arise. In addition, the insurance provides him with facilities to obtain financial assistance enabling him to expand his export business and so help in building up Canada's foreign trade.
Policies of insurance issued under section 21 of the act cover contracts of sale much larger than those normally undertaken by the corporation on its own behalf, and the exporters are not prepared to take on such contracts of sale without insurance protection. Furthermore, the fact that payments are generally spread over a period of years makes it very difficult for exporters to obtain the additional financing required without the support of an export credits insurance policy.
These sales are essential to Canada's wellbeing and materially add to the development of her foreign trade. The practical question of payment often depends more on the over-all balance of payments situation in the country of the buyer, and is more often affected by political considerations in that country than by the normal practices of commercial trade. Where the risk involves political factors that

increase the element of uncertainty in foreign trading and where a contract will prove beneficial to our nation as a whole, it is felt that the people of Canada, through its government, should bear some share of that risk, and by so doing place our exporters in the same position as their competitors in the world market.
