Mr. Chairman, particularly in consequence of the hon. minister's reply to that question, my remarks will be fairly brief. In the first place, this act was before the house for amendment in the earlier session of 1957. I just want to point out that when this act was up for two minor amendments earlier this year some 41 columns of Hansard were utilized by members of the then opposition to discuss certain items of amendment, and naturally I wondered whether or not those who were so critical at that time on the question of whether this corporation should be liable for income tax on its transfers to the underwriting reserve against losses had changed their minds, or whether their proposals then would form part of the amending bill, now that the then critics compose the administration. At that time the Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Health and Welfare, the former member for Simcoe North, and the gentleman, who I believe, has been the acting minister of trade and commerce in the minister's absence, and who has probably been supervising the bill -the hon. member for Greenwood, Minister without Portfolio-were all among those who were so bitter in their denunciation of the amendments made earlier this session.
The other reason for brevity is one that the minister himself has indicated. This bill was introduced in 1944. It was just one of the many wise and farsighted statutes which were prepared by the administration of Mr. Mackenzie King in his desire for the stimulation of postwar trade, for the stabilization of the economy of this country and for the welfare of its people for the post war period. I am very pleased that the minister has paid tribute to the good results of this legislation.
Export Credits Insurance Act
While he did not say so, I am informed that export sales under the ordinary terms of the legislation have assisted by insurance provisions the export of more than $400 million worth of Canadian exports. The minister said that also under section 21 alone export sales beyond $200 million have been assisted. This proposal provides confirmation in my mind of the proof of a statement which appeared in the Time magazine of October 9 when it reproduced a short statement from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix which said this:
The dominant fact in the political life of the country is the Conservatives' close adherence to the Liberals' main lines.
I think that is very true. The minister did give us figures with respect to the amount of export sales that have been assisted by insurance under section 21. He also outlined the provisions of section 21 indicating that this is a special risk that is not solely the responsibility of the board or the corporation but is a risk approved specially by the governor in council. While we are in the committee would he add to the information that is available from the last annual report and tell us what is the latest figure of export sales that have been assisted by the ordinary provisions of the act since December 31, 1956. I believe the annual report indicated that the sales on an ordinary basis were then $376 million.
Recently with respect to this statute I placed some questions on the order paper. I am grateful for certain information that was provided as a result. It was indicated that under section 21, which I take it is our main interest tonight, $104 million in export sales have been insured from January 1, 1957 to October 31, 1957, in other words ten months of this year. I wonder if the minister would tell the committee what proportion of this related to wheat sales and would he indicate with respect to non-wheat sales what the large items of exports were.
I was very interested to read shortly after the introduction of this resolution that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who comes from Saskatchewan visited his home province shortly afterward and made what I thought were rather extravagant statements to the wheat producers respecting the advantages of this particular extension of the total amount of liability that is possible under section 21. The strange thing is that the reports of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in Regina occurred just one day after the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Regina. One got the impression that the total value

Export Credits Insurance Act of the extension of the liability that is possible under this statute by reason of this amending bill would be to the advantage of the wheat producers.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce in Regina on November 15, as I understand it, suggested that we could reasonably anticipate exports of some 300 million bushels of wheat in this crop year. The following day by reason of this particular item of legislation his colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of November 16, indicated that this figure could be upped by 50 million bushels for the same term.
I understand the good reasons when negotiations are taking place why the minister, as he suggested, must be cautious about indicating the countries with which he is now negotiating with respect to possible sales of Canadan wheat. I know this is a competitive thing and I would not want in any way to embarrass these negotiations which are to the benefit of this country but I do think in view of this conflict of estimates within 24 hours in the same city by two members of the government as to the possible sales of wheat for export within the current crop year that this committee is entitled to some explanation.
In particular I would like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to inform the committee-I do not wish to put him on the spot as to the countries with which he is negotiating-whether some 50 million bushels of wheat beyond the 300 million bushels he discussed in Regina are likely to be sold simply because of the insurance provisions that are being provided in this legislation. The reason I ask that is that while the total amount of export sales related to this insurance under section 21 have increased very substantially in the ten months of 1957, according to the returns given to me to which I have previously referred, it actually happens that the amount of wheat insured in the ten months of 1957 is considerably less relatively than wheat sales insured in 1956.
The figures are as follows: Section 21 was utilized in 1956 for sales of wheat to the extent of 24 million bushels. In 1957 the figure is ten million bushels for ten months. I have indicated that in the current

In connection with this amendment I feel I am justified in chastising the Minister of Trade and Commerce a little bit for some remarks he made yesterday. I believe-I think other hon. members will agree with me-he was somewhat flippant when he referred to a possible customer for Canadian wheat, namely Russia. The hon. member for Moose Mountain asked the minister yesterday about the Russian trade delegation presently in Canada. I admit that the minister has been out of Canada recently. It does not seem to me there Is much hope for peace and a quiet life as long as our chief joint occupations with people beyond the iron curtain are to make faces at each other and listen while they call us names.

Generally, as I say, this proposed amendment will be supported by members of the official opposition. In so far as our party is concerned it is simply an extension in liability terms without change, of the principle of good Liberal legislation.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group certainly welcome the fact that the government has seen fit to add another $100 million to the funds available under the Export Credits Insurance Act. I do so particularly because I see a hope that possibly through this measure we will be able to appeal to countries that wish to import our agricultural products to take advantage of this legislation. I hope that the minister-I am confident he will-will invite countries that wish to buy agricultural products from Canada to take advantage of the additional incentive that he has placed in this legislation.
I have particular reference to the question of buying Canadian rape seed. In the past we have sold great amounts of Canadian rape seed. As a matter of fact, it might be of interest to hon. members to know that today Canada is the largest producer of rape seed in the world. I believe it was in 1955 or 1956 that we sold our entire production to Japan, something in the neighbourhood of 40,000 tons. We have not sold any to that country since that time for the simple reason that Japan has not felt that she was in a position to buy because of the shortage of dollars.
Since that time we have had as our major market the United Kingdom and central Europe. Our sales to the United Kingdom have fallen off quite drastically. As I recall, they were in the neighbourhood of 7 thousand tons and I believe that in the past year they fell to approximately 4 thousand or 4J- thousand tons. But we are maintaining our sales to the Scandinavian countries. I am not prepared to say how much those sales amount to but they are considerable. Central Europe is not as interested in buying Canadian rape seed as they were previously, and again I presume it is because of the shortage of United States dollars.
Therefore I hope the minister will invite these countries to take advantage of the opportunities provided under the Export Credits Insurance Act. I also think we have to do something else. If we are going to interest these countries in buying Canadian rape seed products these products must be competitive with the products of the United States. That applies particularly to oil seeds. I am not going to pursue this matter too far. I hope on another occasion to expand the proposition I am going to mention briefly now. I think it falls in line with the wishes and desires of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in that
[Mr. Quelch.l

he has said in effect that he thinks it would be a good thing if we could divert some of the acreage now planted to wheat to some alternative crop or to the raising of livestock, and I entirely agree with him.
I am not sure about the production of rape seed in the whole of Canada but I do know that in Saskatchewan last year we grew in the neighbourhood of half a million acres and it is estimated by Mr. A. D. Miller, the manager of the oil seed processing plant in Saskatoon, that this coming year we could expand that acreage to i| million acres. That would be very desirable if we could market the product and we will only market the product if it is competitive with other oil seeds being offered on the world markets.
Therefore we have to see if we can do something to make the product competitive. The first thing I think we must do, and I believe the minister will agree, is to lower the freight rate on the movement of rape seed from the prairie provinces to the lake-head and to Vancouver. At the present time it is 70 cents a hundred as against 23J cents for flax. It is very unfair, it is discriminatory and causes great hardship for the producers of rape seed. That is only one thing to which we should give consideration if we really want to divert acreage now planted to wheat to some alternative crop.
There is something else I should like to mention to which we must give serious consideration. I refer to the tariff problem existing in this country with relation to oil seeds. We have a potentially great market in this country. Rape seed oil has been under some suspicion because scientists and other people interested in the welfare of the Canadian people have suspected that rape seed contains cholesterol which aggravates heart conditions. But just recently, as a matter of fact in the last month I believe, the national research council issued a report and in that report it is stated quite emphatically as far as they are concerned oil made from rape seed is just as acceptable as any other vegetable oil product. We have a potentially tremendous market in this country and in other countries provided those other countries have the money to buy the product.
I am going to sit down in a moment because I am not going to expand this proposition at this time. There is no tariff on oil seeds or oil processed from such seeds coming into Canada from the United States but there is a substantial tariff on oil seeds and the oil product going into the United States and this situation is causing severe hardship. The people who grow soy beans in Canada must be confronted with the same problem as producers of rape seed.

Here is what is happening. The people in Minnesota and the corn belt of the middle western states who grow soy beans are shipping them into Canada and they are being processed into oil. They can take the oil back to that country if they like but in many cases prior to 1954 they were mixing the United States product with 25 per cent Canadian oil, whether sunflower, soy bean or rape seed oil, and shipping that oil to the United Kingdom thus getting the benefit of the British preferential tariff.
Now that is a pretty deplorable situation. Since, 1954, of course the tariff board has ruled that the mixture must contain not less than 50 per cent Canadian oil, but if that United States product is mixed with 50 per cent Canadian oil it can still be exported to the United Kingdom and be eligible for the British preferential tariff. This is working a real hardship on the producers of this country who are trying to produce an alternative crop in order to receive ready cash.
Now what is the other side of the picture? If we ship rape seed to the United States there is a one cent per pound tariff; if we process rape seed in this country and attempt to ship the oil down there, what do we find? We find on every gallon of oil there is a 5j-cents a gallon tariff plus 2\ cents per pound tariff on that product and yet we allow the US. to export their products into this country, mix it with a percentage of our product, and ship it to the United Kingdom, thereby giving them the opportunity to take advantage of the British preferential tariff. A pretty deplorable state affairs.
This simply means we cannot compete with the United States product. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, we are losing our markets in the United Kingdom and central Europe and I am fairly confident that we are losing them because of the situation 1 have pointed out. I therefore want to suggest to the minister that here we have an opportunity of growing an alternative crop and taking acreage out of wheat production, which is most desirable. First of all however we have to see that our crop is competitive with other crops in other countries. I suggest to the minister that he give some consideration to what I have said in this respect and finally that he invite other countries to take advantage of the act which is now before us in order that we may dispose of some of our surplus agricultural products.

Mr. Chairman, hon. members will notice that this resolution deals with two proposed changes in the National Housing Act; one to increase the amount that is available under section 22 of the act from $250 million to $400 million, and the other to provide for a reduction of down payments. This measure is not designed to be an over-all revision of the National Housing Act. It was not the intention of the government to open the act at all at this session and I gave an answer to that effect to one of the members on orders of the day some weeks ago but the plan which we adopted in August to help in the provision of low-cost homes has been so successful that we now find it necessary to ask for further funds. While doing so we are also asking for a change to lower the down payments because we think that would also be a great help in the provision of housing in Canada at the present time.
I should like to sketch in a bit of background and my first comment would be this. There has been a decline in housing starts from the maximum of 1955. In that year there were 138,000 new housing units started. During 1956 construction was started on a smaller number, namely 127,000 units. It became evident early in 1957 that there would be a further decline in the quantity of new housing started and in the first six months

of this calendar year there were only 48,500 starts as compared with 60,200 in the same period in 1956.
When the new government took over we very soon found that a fear was developing in the homebuilding industry of Canada. Builders were very much concerned. They knew, of course, of this falling away of starts and they thought there would be unemployment in their industry. That fear was spreading back into the lines of activity in Canada which supply the materials for homes including, of course, furniture and other essentials; and certainly there was more depression mindedness, if I may call it that, in the homebuilding industry than possibly any other industry in Canada.
We also found that there was a shortage of low cost homes. There was a real demand for cheaper homes but the trend under the National Housing Act and in the ordinary loan business had been in the direction of more and more expensive homes. I was very much surprised to find that the qualifying income for the average National Housing Act loan made by approved lenders in the month of September of this year was $5,350. The average income for borrowers under the National Housing Act was $5,829. There is some reason for this trend because it is a good deal easier to handle a large loan than it is to handle a small one and I think some preference has been given by the different institutions to the larger loans.

The figure I gave represented the average income of borrowers. Faced with that situation we decided to act and a decision was taken to extend the direct lending of the government. It was our view that money should be found without delay to keep the housebuilding industry in active employment and to maintain the supply of housing for an expanding population. We were especially concerned at the difficulties faced by families of ordinary means in raising mortgage money and, as I said, we decided to extend the direct lending activities of the government.
This is where section 22 of the National Housing Act comes into the picture. It provides the authority for moneys to be advanced to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation out of the consolidated revenue fund to an amount not exceeding $250 million. Such funds have been available to the corporation for making loans. By government policy for some years the corporation has made direct loans for certain specified categories of housing. These were principally in 

the cases of prospective home owners in communities of less than 55,000 population where National Housing Act loans were not available from private lenders approved under the act.
Another type was in the form of loans to limited dividend companies under section 16 of the act for low rental housing. In addition there are other special types of direct loans such as those to primary industries under section 17 and those made to defence workers.
Hon. members will observe that direct loans were not made for ordinary home ownership purposes in the larger urban centres and were not available to house builders producing housing for sale nor, in recent years, for rental. This government source of funds, in fact, had not been used to supplement private National Housing Act investment in the larger cities where the principal supply of new housing is required.
By August of this year about $100 million of the total of $250 million had been used for direct loans, for the purposes which I have mentioned. The government decided at that time that the balance of these moneys- that was roughly $150 million-should immediately be made available in a way that would have the most beneficial effect upon employment in the housing industry and in areas where the need for accommodation was most acute.
We placed certain restrictions on these loans because we felt it was vitally important that they should be used to help people build smaller homes. We were deliberately not trying to give this kind of help for building of the more expensive homes. Restrictions were primarily in the nature of limitation on the floor area. For example, for a three-bedroom bungalow, the floor area allowed was 1,050 square feet. Then, there were other restrictions in the way of not allowing certain features in the home which, while they were very desirable, were not considered as entirely necessary.
As the plan has worked out, the average floor area of bungalows under this agency loan plan is 1,014 square feet which compares with an average of 1,137 square feet for bungalows financed by National Housing Act loans through approved lenders during the year 1957.

It dragged considerably also in the province of British Columbia which should normally take about one-tenth of the total loans across the country. The figure for the west coast province, as of last week, was $8.8 million for 980 units. I do not have the starts under this plan to date. We do not normally get them until the end of the month, but I gave the house figures some days ago and at that time the total starts were 5,992. They will be considerably higher than that at the present time.
From these figures it will be clearly seen that we now require further funds and that is why in these amendments we are asking the house for a further $150 million. I point out that all of that amount will not be available for this low-cost housing plan because, while these activities have been going on, there have also been very extensive activities in the other fields which were covered by section 22, particularly in buildings under the limited
National Housing Act
dividend corporation plan and also in the direct loans in the smaller centres of the country.
I have here the figures for those types of loans as well. For example, under section 16 there have been approvals since the act was first brought in, in 1954,-and that is when the figure of $250 million was set-of $61,368,987, and there are advances under that section being processed of $4,235,948. Under section 17 there have been approvals amounting to $7,020,451, and under section 40- these are direct loans to the smaller centres -amounting to $56,454,565. The additional $150 million, therefore, will have to be used for the purpose of these other types of advances as well as for the small homes. I estimate, however, that there should be from $75 million to $100 million of this additional amount we are asking available for the smaller homes.
So much for that part of this amendment which will provide additional funds. May I now refer to the other part of the amendment which will reduce the down payment under the act. I have several speeches here prepared for me, and it is becoming rather confusing.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, DOWN PAYMENTS, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, DOWN PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is the dangerous part of ad libbing in the middle of these written speeches; I am trying to make my remarks more interesting. The second amendment in the bill is to reduce the down payment which borrowers have to make if they are buying or building a new home under the National Housing Act. In this way it is hoped to make it easier for families of modest means to obtain mortgage money under the act. At present the act provides that a borrower may obtain a loan amounting to 90 per cent of the first $8,000 of lending value and 70 per cent of the lending value in excess of $8,000. The amendment will enable a borrower to obtain a loan amounting to 90 per cent of the first $12,000 of lending value, together with 70 per cent of the lending value in excess of that amount. These larger loans will be available to home owner applicants, to builders and to co-operative housing associations constructing either single family houses or two-family housing units.
These new maximum loan ratios would apply to loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under section 40 of the act under either the agency or the other lending programs. They would also permit approved lenders to make higher ratio insured loans out of their own funds. I have here a table which perhaps hon. members will

National Housing Act allow me to have printed in Hansard which will explain clearly just what these changes would mean. We are not raising the maximum of $12,800. Under the present act where the home has a lending value of $10,000, the loan would be $8,600 and the down payment would be $1,400. Under the proposed amendments the loan would go up from $8,600 to $9,000 and the down payment would go down from $1,400 to $1,000. Where the lending value is now $11,000, the loan would be $9,300 and the down payment $1,700; that is under the law as it is now. Under the proposed change, the loan in such a case would be $9,900 and the down payment $1,100. Where the lending value is $12,000 under the present law, the loan would be $10,000 and the down payment $2,000; under the amendment the loan would be $10,800 and the down payment would be only $1,200. There are other figures in the table which hon. members will see, running up to $16,000 at which figure the down payment would be the same in both cases.
I see it is practically ten o'clock but I am very nearly finished. If hon. members do not object, I will continue.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, DOWN PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: Carry on.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING AGGREGATE AMOUNT AVAILABLE, DOWN PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
One thing I should like to make very clear is that we have had excellent co-operation from builders across the country under the small homes plan. It would be very unfair if they were to be caught now with unsold houses on their hands after we have made this change in the amount of down payment. We propose to see that they do not suffer for that reason. It is planned, therefore, that home owners and builders who are already building under the agency loan program will be permitted to renegotiate their loans so that they can take advantage of the higher loan ratios, provided the loan moneys have not been fully advanced. Similarly, any home owner who has obtained a non-agency loan from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under section 40 and to whom only a portion of the loan so far has been advanced will be eligible to claim a higher loan ratio. In both cases the borrower will have to bear any legal charges associated with the renegotiation of the loan.
Then, as I pointed out, we are not making any increase in the ceiling on loans above the figure of $12,800. There is one other change which will be made by regulation, and that is to raise the proportion of an applicant's income that he can spend for the servicing of his loan. When you lower the down payment, you increase the size of the loan accordingly and there is just that much


more to be paid. In order to give the maximum help to Canadians with smaller incomes we are raising this ratio.
Coupled with this increase in loans it is proposed that there should also be a change in the regulation affecting the relationship between a borrower's income and the loan he may obtain. Up to now an approved lender has been required to obtain approval of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for loans to applicants proposing to assume debt service over 23 per cent of his income. The amended regulation will authorize approved lenders to proceed without special approval up to 27 per cent of income.
Once again, this will help fulfil the government's aim of making housing loans more readily available to families of moderate means. The government believes that there are many borrowers who would be prepared to put a larger proportion of their income into houses if they were able to obtain a home of their own. The direct effect of raising the ratio of debt service to 27 per cent will be to enable more families to qualify for National Housing Act loans.
For example, to qualify without special approval-there is now a provision for special approval by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for higher ratios-at present for a $9,000 loan a borrower has to have an income of about $4,050. I should say that the actual income required will depend upon the size of municipal taxes, but I am taking $240 as a representative municipal tax figure for the purpose of this example.
Under the 27 per cent rule it will only be necessary to have an income of $3,450 to qualify for a loan of this size. In other words, the income requirement would come down from $4,050 to $3,450.
Similarly, under the new down payment arrangement a borrower can obtain a $12,200 loan on a $14,000 house but with existing regulations regarding the size of debt service he would require an income of nearly $5,200 a year to qualify for a $12,200 loan. When the 27 per cent rule takes effect an income of $4,360 a year will be sufficient.
This change will be made by changing the regulations, not by amending the act. Quite frankly, I should like to be able to help an income group even lower than those who will be helped by this legislation.
Finally, the objectives of these amendments and of the change in regulations are to provide homes for the lower income groups and to raise the morale of the home building industry and all the associate industries. In that regard I think hon. members will agree that our existing plan has already gone quite far in the direction of achieving

that objective. The objective is also to furnish employment because the building of all these homes at this time means a great many thousands of additional jobs in Canada. Above all, the objective is to build a better Canada.
As I said in opening my remarks, many other plans are under study by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We would be very glad to have the co-operation of private members of the house. Some of the private members on the government side were very interested in housing and they asked to be given the opportunity to study the whole housing question. They have been doing that with the co-operation of the corporation's officials. Private members of the official opposition have made the same request and they have been given exactly the same facilities. We would be glad to extend those facilities to the members of the other two parties who might be interested in carrying out such a study because these are complicated questions. I do not pretend to know half the answers myself and we want all the help we can get.
I should like to close with a word of commendation for the splendid work done in the field of housing by my predecessor,
National Housing Act
the Hon. Robert Winters. He and I were friends from the time he first came into the house. I always admired him greatly even though criticizing him pretty severely at times. I realized how much effort he was putting into this job and when I took over the department I was not a bit surprised to find that he had really done a first class job in the housing field. I doubt whether he always got the support from the government that he would have liked. However, sometimes we all have these troubles, I suppose.

The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Did any thefts of postal stamps, money orders, postal notes, cash or otherwise, occur in the different post offices of Canada from June 21, 1957 to date? If so, how many?
2.	What was the total sum involved and what new measures if any have been taken by the Post Office Department to prevent such incidents?
Answer by: Hon. W. M. Hamillon (Postmaster
General):
1.	Yes; there were 143 cases where post offices were broken into and in 63 of these cases no cash or postal supplies were stolen.
2.	The amount of cash stolen was $10,742. In addition, postage stamps, unemployment insurance stamps, postal scrip and money order forms were stolen. The postage stamps and unemployment insurance stamps do not represent a loss unless they are used. Money order forms do not represent a loss unless they are cashed at post offices.
Security measures now being taken:
(a)	Continuation of the program for gradual replacement of all safes in post offices occupying premises provided by the Department of Public Works with new type safes designed in co-operation with the R.C.M.P.
(b)	In the planning of new post office buildings, provision is made for a built-in "strong room" containing a burglar-resistant money chest for the cash.
(c)	In April of this year, agreement was reached with the Department of Public Works for the installation of glass "ports" in mail lobby doors for new post office buildings. This is to enable our employees to identify callers before opening the mail lobby doors. On doors already installed without ports, provision has been made for the installation of security chains and this program is being carried out at district level.
(d)	On June 20 as a result of an agreement with the Department of Public Works, field officers were instructed to arrange with local district architects for the removal of casters on post office safes and where considered practicable have these safes bolted to the floor to increase the difficulty of their illegal removal.
(e)	The use of night depository service at banks is being continually extended to reduce the amount of cash held overnight.
(f)	Security transfer services are used where necessary to transfer larger amounts.

Question No. 168-Mr. Christian:
What steps have been taken by the government since June 10, 1957, to help the lumbering industry in the province of British Columbia, and especially the small loggers who face adverse market conditions?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister
of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	The government has already made available for housing loan purposes $150,000,000 and has placed a resolution before the House of Commons which would provide a further $150,000,000 for these purposes. These steps are of substantial indirect assistance to the building industry as with an increase in housing construction will come an increased demand for timber and timber products.
2.	An agreement was entered into with the government of the province of British Columbia whereby the government of Canada will pay one-third of the cost of spraying forests in the northern part of Vancouver island to combat an outbreak of the blackheaded budworm. Present indications are that the federal contribution will exceed $83,000.
3.	An agreement was entered into with the government of the province of British Columbia whereby the government of Canada will contribute, mainly on a 50 per cent basis, toward the cost of capital expenditures made by the province for equipment, roads, etc., required for forest fire protection. It is expected that the federal contribution for 1957-58 will be over $74,000.
4.	Indirect assistance is being given through the program of forest research carried on by the federal government in British Columbia including the work of the forest products laboratory at Vancouver. Expenditures in 1957-58 will likely exceed $250,000.
